description: Trusted local reference corpus for the PS2 Source Verification Layer. Every entry is a short, verifiable statement with a named source. This file is the ONLY grounding evidence PS2 uses - no external knowledge API is called. Version 2.0 extends the original linked-list-centred corpus to the fundamentals of each supported computer-science area and to basic mathematics. Every sentence names its own subject (no pronouns), because contradiction checks compare clause with clause. The corpus is still incomplete by nature: a claim with no matching entry is reported as unsupported/unverifiable and routed to REVIEW, never auto-failed.

entries.title: Singly linked list reversal
entries.text: Reversing a singly linked list iteratively requires three pointers (previous, current, next) and runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space. Each node's next pointer is redirected to its predecessor while traversing the list once.
entries.source: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, 3rd edition, Chapter 10

entries.title: Recursive linked list reversal space cost
entries.text: A recursive reversal of a singly linked list uses O(n) space because each of the n recursive calls occupies a stack frame. It is not a constant-space solution.
entries.source: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, 3rd edition, Chapter 10

entries.title: Reversing a linked list in groups of k
entries.text: Reversing a singly linked list in groups of k nodes runs in O(n) time. Each group of k nodes is reversed independently and the group boundaries are re-linked. When fewer than k nodes remain, they are conventionally left in their original order.
entries.source: LeetCode problem 25, Reverse Nodes in k-Group

entries.title: Linked list traversal is sequential
entries.text: A singly linked list does not support random access. Reaching the i-th element requires traversing i nodes from the head, so indexed access costs O(n), unlike an array which costs O(1).
entries.source: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, 3rd edition, Chapter 10

entries.title: Binary search requires a sorted array
entries.text: Binary search runs in O(log n) time but only works on a sorted sequence with random access. On an unsorted array it gives incorrect results, and on a linked list it loses its advantage because seeking the midpoint costs O(n).
entries.source: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, 3rd edition, Chapter 12

entries.title: Comparison sort lower bound
entries.text: Any comparison-based sorting algorithm needs at least O(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Merge sort and heap sort achieve this bound; quicksort averages O(n log n) but degrades to O(n^2) in the worst case.
entries.source: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, 3rd edition, Chapter 8

entries.title: Hash table average and worst case
entries.text: Hash table lookup, insertion and deletion average O(1) time. The worst case degrades to O(n) when many keys collide into the same bucket, for example under a poor hash function or an adversarial key set.
entries.source: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, 3rd edition, Chapter 11

entries.title: Stack and queue ordering
entries.text: A stack is a last-in, first-out (LIFO) structure supporting push and pop at one end. A queue is first-in, first-out (FIFO), with enqueue at the rear and dequeue at the front. Both support these operations in O(1) time.
entries.source: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, 3rd edition, Chapter 10

entries.title: Binary search tree operation costs
entries.text: Binary search tree search, insert and delete cost O(h) where h is the tree height. For a balanced tree h is O(log n), but an unbalanced tree can degenerate to a linked list with h equal to n, making operations O(n).
entries.source: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, 3rd edition, Chapter 12

entries.title: Breadth-first and depth-first search
entries.text: Breadth-first search explores a graph level by level using a queue and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. Depth-first search explores as deep as possible using a stack or recursion. Both run in O(V + E) time on an adjacency list.
entries.source: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, 3rd edition, Chapter 22

entries.title: Dijkstra's algorithm and negative weights
entries.text: Dijkstra's algorithm computes single-source shortest paths in O((V + E) log V) time with a binary heap, but it requires non-negative edge weights. Graphs with negative edges need the Bellman-Ford algorithm instead.
entries.source: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, 3rd edition, Chapter 24

entries.title: Detecting a cycle in a linked list
entries.text: Floyd's cycle detection algorithm, also called the tortoise and hare, detects a loop in a linked list using two pointers moving at different speeds. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.
entries.source: Floyd, Non-deterministic Algorithms, JACM 1967

entries.title: Python list is a dynamic array
entries.text: A Python list is implemented as a dynamic array, not a linked list. Appending is amortised O(1), indexing is O(1), and inserting or deleting at the front is O(n) because later elements must shift.
entries.source: CPython source, Objects/listobject.c

entries.title: In-place algorithms and auxiliary space
entries.text: An in-place algorithm uses O(1) auxiliary space beyond its input. Iterative linked list reversal is in-place; creating a new list of the reversed nodes is not, because it allocates O(n) additional memory.
entries.source: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, 3rd edition

entries.title: Doubly linked list trade-offs
entries.text: A doubly linked list stores both next and previous pointers, allowing O(1) deletion given a node reference and bidirectional traversal, at the cost of one extra pointer of memory per node.
entries.source: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms, 3rd edition, Chapter 10

entries.title: Power rule for derivatives
entries.text: The power rule states that the derivative of x^n with respect to x is n*x^(n-1) for any real number n. The derivative of a constant is zero, and differentiation is linear.
entries.source: Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th edition

entries.title: Quadratic formula and discriminant
entries.text: The roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a non-zero are given by x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a). The discriminant b^2 - 4ac determines the nature of the roots: positive gives two distinct real roots, zero gives one repeated real root, and negative gives two complex conjugate roots.
entries.source: Stewart, Precalculus, 7th edition

entries.title: Pythagorean theorem
entries.text: In a right-angled triangle the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides: a^2 + b^2 = c^2. It applies only to right-angled triangles in Euclidean geometry.
entries.source: Euclid, Elements, Book I, Proposition 47

entries.title: Mean, median and outliers
entries.text: The arithmetic mean is the sum of values divided by their count. The median is the middle value of the sorted data. The median is more robust to outliers than the mean, because a single extreme value shifts the mean but barely moves the median.
entries.source: Moore, Introduction to the Practice of Statistics, 9th edition

entries.title: Probability axioms
entries.text: A probability is a real number between 0 and 1 inclusive. The probabilities of all mutually exclusive outcomes in a sample space sum to 1. For independent events A and B, P(A and B) = P(A) * P(B).
entries.source: Ross, A First Course in Probability, 9th edition

entries.title: Matrix multiplication dimensions
entries.text: Matrix multiplication is defined for an m-by-n matrix times an n-by-p matrix, producing an m-by-p result. It is associative and distributive but not commutative: A*B generally does not equal B*A.
entries.source: Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra, 5th edition

entries.title: Hydrogen bonding and water's boiling point
entries.text: Water has an unusually high boiling point of 100 degrees Celsius at standard atmospheric pressure because its molecules form hydrogen bonds. Methane, which has a similar molar mass but cannot hydrogen bond, boils at about -161 degrees Celsius.
entries.source: Atkins, Physical Chemistry, 11th edition

entries.title: Newton's second law
entries.text: Newton's second law states that the net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration, F = ma. Force is measured in newtons, mass in kilograms and acceleration in metres per second squared.
entries.source: Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, 10th edition

entries.title: Photosynthesis inputs and outputs
entries.text: Photosynthesis in green plants converts carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen using light energy captured by chlorophyll. The overall reaction is 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy -> C6H12O6 + 6O2.
entries.source: Campbell Biology, 11th edition, Chapter 10

entries.title: Speed of light in vacuum
entries.text: The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 metres per second by definition of the metre. Light travels more slowly in any material medium, which is what refractive index measures.
entries.source: BIPM, SI Brochure, 9th edition

entries.title: Cell membrane structure
entries.text: The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins, described by the fluid mosaic model. It is selectively permeable, controlling which substances enter and leave the cell.
entries.source: Campbell Biology, 11th edition, Chapter 7

entries.title: Insulin and blood glucose
entries.text: Insulin is a hormone produced by the beta cells of the pancreatic islets. It lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake into muscle and fat tissue and by stimulating glycogen synthesis in the liver. Glucagon raises blood glucose and opposes insulin.
entries.source: Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th edition

entries.title: Normal resting heart rate in adults
entries.text: A normal resting heart rate for a healthy adult is between 60 and 100 beats per minute. Well-trained endurance athletes can have resting rates below 60, which is not pathological in that context.
entries.source: American Heart Association clinical guidance

entries.title: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes
entries.text: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing absolute insulin deficiency. Type 2 diabetes involves insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency and is strongly associated with obesity and physical inactivity.
entries.source: World Health Organization, Classification of Diabetes Mellitus, 2019

entries.title: Break-even point formula
entries.text: The break-even point in units equals fixed costs divided by the contribution margin per unit, where contribution margin is the selling price per unit minus the variable cost per unit. Below this volume the business makes a loss.
entries.source: Horngren, Cost Accounting: A Managerial Emphasis, 16th edition

entries.title: Gross margin definition
entries.text: Gross margin is revenue minus cost of goods sold, usually expressed as a percentage of revenue. It measures production profitability and excludes operating expenses such as marketing, administration and research.
entries.source: Horngren, Cost Accounting: A Managerial Emphasis, 16th edition

entries.title: Law of supply and demand
entries.text: In a competitive market, an increase in price generally reduces quantity demanded and increases quantity supplied. Market equilibrium occurs at the price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.
entries.source: Mankiw, Principles of Economics, 8th edition

entries.title: Subject and predicate
entries.text: Every complete English sentence has a subject, which names what the sentence is about, and a predicate, which contains the verb and states something about the subject. In 'The old library closed last winter', the subject is 'The old library' and the predicate is 'closed last winter'.
entries.source: Huddleston and Pullum, The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language

entries.title: Active and passive voice
entries.text: In the active voice the subject performs the action, as in 'The committee approved the plan'. In the passive voice the subject receives it, as in 'The plan was approved by the committee'. The passive is formed with a form of 'to be' plus a past participle.
entries.source: Huddleston and Pullum, The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language

entries.title: The Seine in Paris
entries.text: The Seine is the river that flows through Paris, France. It divides the city into the Right Bank and the Left Bank, and historically served as the principal trade route that shaped the city's development.
entries.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, entry: Seine River

entries.title: Structure of the United Nations
entries.text: The United Nations was founded in 1945 and has six principal organs, including the General Assembly and the Security Council. The Security Council has five permanent members with veto power: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States.
entries.source: United Nations Charter, 1945

entries.title: Binary search
entries.text: Binary search finds a target in a sorted array by repeatedly comparing it with the middle element and continuing in the half that can still contain it. Iterative binary search runs in O(log n) time and uses O(1) extra space.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Recursive binary search
entries.text: A recursive binary search calls itself on the left or right half of the range. Recursive binary search runs in O(log n) time and uses O(log n) stack space for the recursive calls.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Linear search
entries.text: Linear search checks each element in turn until it finds the target or reaches the end. Linear search works on unsorted data and runs in O(n) time in the worst case.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Merge sort
entries.text: Merge sort divides the array into two halves, sorts each half recursively and merges the two sorted halves. Merge sort runs in O(n log n) time in the best, average and worst case. Merge sort needs O(n) extra space for merging and is a stable sort.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Quicksort
entries.text: Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions the array into elements smaller and larger than the pivot, and sorts the two parts recursively. Quicksort runs in O(n log n) time on average. Quicksort runs in O(n^2) time in the worst case, which happens when the pivots are badly unbalanced.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Bubble sort and insertion sort
entries.text: Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent elements that are out of order, and insertion sort inserts each element into its place in the sorted part before it. Bubble sort runs in O(n^2) time in the worst case. Insertion sort runs in O(n^2) time in the worst case and in O(n) time on an array that is already sorted.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Primality testing by trial division
entries.text: A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. Trial division tests whether n is prime by trying divisors from 2 up to the square root of n, and runs in O(sqrt(n)) time. The numbers 0 and 1 are not prime, and 2 is the only even prime number.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Factorial
entries.text: The factorial of a non-negative integer n, written n!, is the product of all positive integers up to n, and 0! is defined as 1. The factorial can be computed with a loop or recursively using n! = n * (n-1)!, and either way takes O(n) time.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Recursion and the call stack
entries.text: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input and needs a base case to stop. Each recursive call adds a frame to the call stack, so a recursion of depth n uses O(n) stack space and can overflow the stack if the recursion is too deep.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Big-O notation
entries.text: Big-O notation describes an upper bound on how an algorithm's running time or memory grows with the input size n, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Dynamic programming
entries.text: Dynamic programming solves a problem by combining solutions to overlapping subproblems and storing each result so that it is computed only once, either top-down with memoisation or bottom-up with a table.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Greedy algorithms
entries.text: A greedy algorithm builds a solution step by step, always taking the choice that looks best at that moment. A greedy algorithm is correct only for problems where locally optimal choices lead to a global optimum.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Euclid's algorithm
entries.text: Euclid's algorithm computes the greatest common divisor of two integers by repeatedly replacing the pair (a, b) with (b, a mod b) until b is zero; the remaining a is the greatest common divisor.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Stack
entries.text: A stack is a last-in, first-out data structure. Push adds an element to the top of the stack and pop removes the element from the top of the stack. Stack push and pop each take O(1) time.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Stack with minimum retrieval
entries.text: A stack can return its minimum element in O(1) time by keeping a second stack of minimums: each push records the smaller of the new value and the current minimum, and each pop removes from both stacks.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Queue
entries.text: A queue is a first-in, first-out data structure. Enqueue adds an element at the back of the queue and dequeue removes the element at the front of the queue. Queue enqueue and dequeue each take O(1) time.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Queue built from two stacks
entries.text: A queue can be implemented with two stacks: enqueue pushes onto the first stack, and dequeue pops from the second stack, moving every element across from the first stack only when the second stack is empty. Each operation of a queue built from two stacks takes amortised O(1) time.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Arrays and linked lists
entries.text: An array stores elements in contiguous memory and gives O(1) access by index, but inserting or deleting in the middle takes O(n) time. A linked list gives O(1) insertion and deletion at a known node but O(n) access by position.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Binary heap and priority queue
entries.text: A binary heap is a complete binary tree in which every parent is ordered with respect to its children. A binary heap supports inserting an element and removing the minimum or maximum in O(log n) time, and is the usual implementation of a priority queue.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Graph representations
entries.text: A graph can be stored as an adjacency list, which uses O(V + E) space, or as an adjacency matrix, which uses O(V^2) space and answers whether an edge exists in O(1) time.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: Balanced binary search trees
entries.text: A balanced binary search tree, such as an AVL tree or a red-black tree, keeps its height at O(log n), so search, insertion and deletion all take O(log n) time in the worst case.
entries.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms

entries.title: GROUP BY and aggregate functions
entries.text: In SQL, GROUP BY collects rows that share the same values in the listed columns into groups, and aggregate functions such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX compute one value for each group.
entries.source: Elmasri and Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems

entries.title: WHERE and HAVING
entries.text: In SQL, WHERE filters individual rows before they are grouped, while HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can use aggregate functions such as COUNT.
entries.source: Elmasri and Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems

entries.title: Finding duplicate values in SQL
entries.text: Duplicate values in a column can be found by grouping on that column and keeping the groups with more than one row: SELECT email, COUNT(*) FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.
entries.source: Elmasri and Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems

entries.title: Second highest value in SQL
entries.text: The second highest value in a column can be found with a subquery that takes the maximum of the values below the overall maximum: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees). It can also be found by ordering the distinct values in descending order and skipping the first with LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1.
entries.source: Elmasri and Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems

entries.title: Primary and foreign keys
entries.text: A primary key uniquely identifies each row of a table and cannot be NULL. A foreign key is a column that refers to the primary key of another table and enforces referential integrity between the two tables.
entries.source: Elmasri and Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems

entries.title: SQL joins
entries.text: An INNER JOIN returns only the rows that have a match in both tables. A LEFT JOIN returns every row of the left table, with NULLs in the right table's columns where there is no match.
entries.source: Elmasri and Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems

entries.title: Database indexes
entries.text: A database index, commonly a B-tree, lets the database find rows by the indexed column without scanning the whole table. A database index speeds up reads but takes extra storage and slows down inserts, updates and deletes.
entries.source: Elmasri and Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems

entries.title: Normalisation
entries.text: Normalisation organises a relational schema to reduce redundancy. First normal form requires atomic column values, second normal form removes partial dependencies on a composite key, and third normal form removes transitive dependencies.
entries.source: Elmasri and Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems

entries.title: ACID transactions
entries.text: A database transaction is ACID: atomic (all of it happens or none of it), consistent (it preserves the database's rules), isolated (concurrent transactions do not interfere) and durable (committed changes survive a crash).
entries.source: Elmasri and Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems

entries.title: Round-robin scheduling
entries.text: Round-robin CPU scheduling gives each process in the ready queue a fixed time slice called a time quantum, in turn. In round-robin scheduling a process that does not finish within its time quantum is preempted and moved to the back of the ready queue, and the scheduler runs the process at the front of the ready queue next. Round-robin scheduling is preemptive.
entries.source: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts

entries.title: Choosing the time quantum
entries.text: In round-robin scheduling a very small time quantum causes many context switches and high overhead, while a very large quantum makes round-robin behave like first-come, first-served scheduling.
entries.source: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts

entries.title: First-come, first-served and shortest-job-first
entries.text: First-come, first-served scheduling runs processes in the order they arrive and is non-preemptive. Shortest-job-first scheduling runs the process with the shortest next CPU burst. Shortest-job-first scheduling gives the minimum average waiting time but can starve long processes.
entries.source: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts

entries.title: Processes and threads
entries.text: A process is a running program with its own address space. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process; threads of the same process share its memory and resources but each has its own stack and program counter.
entries.source: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts

entries.title: Context switch
entries.text: A context switch saves the state of the running process or thread and restores the state of another so that it can run. Context switches are pure overhead because no user work is done during the switch.
entries.source: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts

entries.title: Deadlock and its four conditions
entries.text: A deadlock is a state in which a set of processes are each waiting for a resource held by another process in the set, so none can proceed. A deadlock can occur only if four conditions hold at the same time: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.
entries.source: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts

entries.title: Handling deadlock
entries.text: Deadlock can be prevented by ensuring at least one of the four necessary conditions cannot hold, avoided by granting resources only when the system stays in a safe state, or detected and then recovered from by terminating or rolling back processes.
entries.source: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts

entries.title: Virtual memory and paging
entries.text: Virtual memory gives each process its own address space, which the operating system maps onto physical memory in fixed-size pages. A page fault occurs when a process accesses a page that is not in physical memory, and the operating system then loads it from disk.
entries.source: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts

entries.title: Race conditions and mutual exclusion
entries.text: A race condition occurs when the result depends on the timing of threads that access shared data. A mutex or semaphore protects a critical section so that only one thread executes it at a time.
entries.source: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts

entries.title: TCP and UDP
entries.text: TCP is a connection-oriented transport protocol that provides reliable, in-order delivery with flow control and congestion control. UDP is a connectionless transport protocol that provides unreliable delivery with no ordering or congestion control, but UDP has lower overhead than TCP.
entries.source: Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach

entries.title: TCP three-way handshake
entries.text: A TCP connection is established with a three-way handshake: the client sends SYN, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client answers with ACK.
entries.source: Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach

entries.title: TCP slow start
entries.text: In TCP slow start the congestion window starts at a small value, typically one maximum segment size, and the congestion window increases by one segment for every acknowledgement received, which doubles the congestion window every round-trip time, so the growth in slow start is exponential. Slow start continues until the window reaches the slow start threshold (ssthresh) or a loss is detected.
entries.source: Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach

entries.title: TCP congestion avoidance
entries.text: In TCP congestion avoidance, which begins once the congestion window reaches the slow start threshold, the congestion window increases linearly by about one maximum segment size per round-trip time. Congestion avoidance is the additive-increase part of additive increase, multiplicative decrease (AIMD).
entries.source: Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach

entries.title: TCP reaction to loss
entries.text: When TCP detects loss by a timeout, it sets the slow start threshold to half the current congestion window, resets the congestion window to one segment and re-enters slow start. When loss is detected by three duplicate acknowledgements, TCP Reno halves the congestion window and continues in congestion avoidance (fast recovery).
entries.source: Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach

entries.title: TCP congestion control overview
entries.text: TCP congestion control limits the sending rate with a congestion window, so that a sender does not overwhelm the network. The sender probes for available capacity with slow start and congestion avoidance and reduces the window when it detects packet loss.
entries.source: Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach

entries.title: DNS resolution
entries.text: DNS translates a domain name into an IP address. A DNS client asks a recursive resolver, which, if the answer is not cached, queries a root name server, then the top-level domain name server, then the authoritative name server for the domain, and returns the IP address to the client. DNS answers are cached for the time-to-live of the record.
entries.source: Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach

entries.title: HTTP methods and status codes
entries.text: HTTP is a stateless request-response protocol. GET retrieves a resource and POST submits data to the server. Status codes in the 200s indicate success, 300s redirection, 400s a client error and 500s a server error.
entries.source: Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach

entries.title: IP addresses
entries.text: An IPv4 address is 32 bits long and is usually written as four decimal numbers separated by dots. An IPv6 address is 128 bits long. A subnet mask separates the network part of an address from the host part.
entries.source: Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach

entries.title: HTTPS and TLS
entries.text: HTTPS is HTTP sent over TLS. TLS encrypts the connection and authenticates the server with a certificate, using asymmetric cryptography to agree a shared key and symmetric encryption for the data.
entries.source: Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach

entries.title: k-nearest neighbours classification
entries.text: The k-nearest neighbours algorithm classifies a new data point by finding the k training points closest to it, usually by Euclidean distance, and assigning the class that is most common among those k neighbours (a majority vote). The k-nearest neighbours algorithm has no training phase beyond storing the training data.
entries.source: James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning

entries.title: Choosing k in k-nearest neighbours
entries.text: In k-nearest neighbours a small k makes the model sensitive to noise and prone to overfitting, while a large k smooths the decision boundary and can underfit. Features should be scaled, because the distance is dominated by features with large ranges.
entries.source: James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning

entries.title: Classification and regression
entries.text: In supervised learning, classification predicts a discrete class label and regression predicts a continuous numeric value. Both are trained on labelled examples.
entries.source: James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning

entries.title: Supervised and unsupervised learning
entries.text: Supervised learning trains on examples that include the correct output label. Unsupervised learning, such as clustering, finds structure in data that has no labels.
entries.source: James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning

entries.title: Overfitting
entries.text: Overfitting occurs when a model fits the noise in its training data rather than the underlying pattern, so an overfitted model performs well on the training data but poorly on new, unseen data. Overfitting is more likely with a complex model and little training data.
entries.source: James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning

entries.title: Regularisation
entries.text: Regularisation reduces overfitting by adding a penalty on the size of the model's weights to the loss function, which discourages overly complex models. L2 (ridge) regularisation penalises the squared weights and shrinks them towards zero; L1 (lasso) penalises their absolute values and can set some weights exactly to zero.
entries.source: James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning

entries.title: Training, validation and test sets
entries.text: A model is fitted on the training set, tuned on a validation set and finally evaluated on a test set that was not used for fitting or tuning. Cross-validation repeats this by rotating which part of the data is held out.
entries.source: James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning

entries.title: Bias-variance trade-off
entries.text: A model that is too simple has high bias and underfits; a model that is too complex has high variance and overfits. The bias-variance trade-off is the balance between the two.
entries.source: James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning

entries.title: k-means clustering
entries.text: k-means is an unsupervised clustering algorithm. k-means assigns each point to the nearest of k centroids, recomputes each centroid as the mean of its points, and repeats until the assignments stop changing.
entries.source: James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning

entries.title: Gradient descent
entries.text: Gradient descent minimises a loss function by repeatedly moving the parameters a small step in the direction of the negative gradient. The step size is set by the learning rate.
entries.source: James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning

entries.title: Precision and recall
entries.text: Precision is the fraction of predicted positives that are actually positive. Recall is the fraction of actual positives that the model finds. A confusion matrix counts true and false positives and negatives.
entries.source: James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning

entries.title: Unit testing
entries.text: Unit testing checks the smallest testable parts of a program, such as a single function or class, in isolation from the rest of the system. Dependencies are often replaced by mocks or stubs, so unit tests are fast and pinpoint the faulty unit.
entries.source: Sommerville, Software Engineering

entries.title: Integration testing
entries.text: Integration testing checks that separately developed units or modules work correctly together, and finds defects in the interfaces and interactions between them, such as calls to a database or another service.
entries.source: Sommerville, Software Engineering

entries.title: Unit testing versus integration testing
entries.text: Unit tests verify one component in isolation and are fast and narrow in scope; integration tests verify the interaction between several components and are slower and broader. Integration testing is normally carried out after unit testing.
entries.source: Sommerville, Software Engineering

entries.title: Other levels of testing
entries.text: System testing checks the complete, integrated system against its requirements. Acceptance testing checks that it meets the user's needs. Regression testing re-runs existing tests after a change to confirm that nothing that used to work has broken.
entries.source: Sommerville, Software Engineering

entries.title: Test-driven development
entries.text: In test-driven development a failing test is written first, then the minimum code to make it pass, and then the code is refactored while the tests are kept passing.
entries.source: Sommerville, Software Engineering

entries.title: Refactoring
entries.text: Refactoring changes the internal structure of code to make it easier to understand and modify without changing its external behaviour.
entries.source: Sommerville, Software Engineering

entries.title: Continuous integration
entries.text: In continuous integration developers merge their changes into a shared branch frequently, and each merge triggers an automated build and test run so that integration problems are found early.
entries.source: Sommerville, Software Engineering

entries.title: Waterfall and agile
entries.text: The waterfall model carries out requirements, design, implementation, testing and maintenance as sequential phases. Agile methods deliver software in short iterations and adapt the plan to feedback after each one.
entries.source: Sommerville, Software Engineering

entries.title: Git merge
entries.text: git merge combines two branches by creating a new merge commit that has both branch tips as parents. A git merge preserves the existing commits and the full history of both branches. If the target branch has not moved, Git performs a fast-forward instead of creating a merge commit.
entries.source: Chacon and Straub, Pro Git

entries.title: Git rebase
entries.text: git rebase moves the commits of one branch so that they start from the tip of another branch, re-applying each commit and creating new commits with new hashes. The result of a git rebase is a linear history without a merge commit.
entries.source: Chacon and Straub, Pro Git

entries.title: Merge versus rebase
entries.text: Merging preserves history exactly as it happened and is safe on shared branches. Rebasing rewrites history, so commits that have already been pushed and shared with others should not be rebased.
entries.source: Chacon and Straub, Pro Git

entries.title: The HTML form element
entries.text: The HTML form element groups input controls that collect data from a user. The form's action attribute gives the URL the data is sent to and the form's method attribute chooses the HTTP method, GET or POST.
entries.source: MDN Web Docs

entries.title: Form inputs and labels
entries.text: An HTML input element's type attribute sets the kind of control, for example text, email or password, and its name attribute is the key under which the value is submitted. A label element is associated with an input through its for attribute, which must match the input's id.
entries.source: MDN Web Docs

entries.title: HTML form validation
entries.text: The required attribute makes the browser refuse to submit a form while that field is empty. An input of type email is checked by the browser to contain a correctly formatted email address.
entries.source: MDN Web Docs

entries.title: GET and POST form submission
entries.text: A form submitted with GET appends the field values to the URL as a query string. A form submitted with POST sends them in the body of the request, which is appropriate for sensitive or large data.
entries.source: MDN Web Docs

entries.title: Centring with flexbox
entries.text: A flex container centres its child horizontally and vertically with display: flex, justify-content: center and align-items: center. justify-content aligns items along the main axis and align-items along the cross axis.
entries.source: MDN Web Docs

entries.title: The CSS box model
entries.text: In the CSS box model every element is a box made of its content, padding, border and margin. With box-sizing: border-box the width and height include the padding and border.
entries.source: MDN Web Docs

entries.title: CSS selectors and specificity
entries.text: A CSS class selector starts with a dot and an id selector with a hash sign. When rules conflict, an id selector is more specific than a class selector, which is more specific than an element selector.
entries.source: MDN Web Docs

entries.title: Semantic HTML
entries.text: Semantic HTML elements such as header, nav, main, article and footer describe the meaning of their content, which improves accessibility and helps search engines.
entries.source: MDN Web Docs

entries.title: Responsive design
entries.text: Responsive web design adapts a page's layout to the size of the screen, using flexible layouts and CSS media queries that apply rules only at certain viewport widths.
entries.source: MDN Web Docs

entries.title: Encapsulation
entries.text: Encapsulation bundles an object's data with the methods that operate on it and hides the internal state behind a public interface.
entries.source: Booch et al., Object-Oriented Analysis and Design with Applications

entries.title: Inheritance
entries.text: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and extend the attributes and methods of a superclass, and models an is-a relationship.
entries.source: Booch et al., Object-Oriented Analysis and Design with Applications

entries.title: Polymorphism
entries.text: Polymorphism lets code call the same method on objects of different classes, with each class providing its own implementation, typically by overriding a method of a shared superclass or interface.
entries.source: Booch et al., Object-Oriented Analysis and Design with Applications

entries.title: Abstraction and interfaces
entries.text: An interface declares methods without implementing them, and an abstract class can provide some implementation but cannot be instantiated. Both let code depend on what an object does rather than how.
entries.source: Booch et al., Object-Oriented Analysis and Design with Applications

entries.title: Composition over inheritance
entries.text: Composition builds a class from other objects it holds as fields, modelling a has-a relationship. Composition is often preferred to inheritance because composition couples classes less tightly.
entries.source: Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, Design Patterns

entries.title: CPU cache
entries.text: A CPU cache is a small, fast memory that holds copies of recently used data from main memory. A CPU cache works because programs show locality of reference. A cache miss occurs when the requested data is not in the cache.
entries.source: Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design

entries.title: Instruction pipelining
entries.text: Pipelining splits instruction execution into stages such as fetch, decode, execute, memory access and write-back, so that several instructions are processed at once, which raises throughput.
entries.source: Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design

entries.title: Von Neumann architecture
entries.text: In the von Neumann architecture, program instructions and data are stored in the same memory, and the processor repeats a fetch-decode-execute cycle.
entries.source: Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design

entries.title: RISC and CISC
entries.text: A RISC processor uses a small set of simple, fixed-length instructions, while a CISC processor has many complex instructions of varying length.
entries.source: Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design

entries.title: Compiled and interpreted languages
entries.text: A compiler translates the whole source program into machine code before it runs. An interpreter executes the program statement by statement without producing a separate machine-code file.
entries.source: Sebesta, Concepts of Programming Languages

entries.title: Static and dynamic typing
entries.text: In a statically typed language the type of every variable is checked at compile time. In a dynamically typed language types are checked at run time and a variable can hold values of different types.
entries.source: Sebesta, Concepts of Programming Languages

entries.title: Garbage collection
entries.text: Garbage collection automatically reclaims memory that the program can no longer reach, so the programmer does not free it manually.
entries.source: Sebesta, Concepts of Programming Languages

entries.title: Pass by value and pass by reference
entries.text: With pass by value a function receives a copy of the argument, so changes inside the function do not affect the caller's variable. With pass by reference the function works on the caller's variable itself.
entries.source: Sebesta, Concepts of Programming Languages

entries.title: Cloud service models
entries.text: Infrastructure as a Service provides virtual machines, storage and networks; Platform as a Service provides a managed platform for deploying applications; Software as a Service delivers a complete application over the internet.
entries.source: NIST SP 800-145, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing

entries.title: Horizontal and vertical scaling
entries.text: Vertical scaling adds more CPU or memory to an existing machine. Horizontal scaling adds more machines and spreads the load across them, usually behind a load balancer.
entries.source: General reference: widely documented cloud computing fundamentals

entries.title: Containers and virtual machines
entries.text: A virtual machine runs a full guest operating system on a hypervisor. A container shares the host's operating system kernel and isolates only the application and its dependencies, so it is lighter and starts faster.
entries.source: General reference: widely documented cloud computing fundamentals

entries.title: Serverless computing
entries.text: In serverless computing the provider runs code in response to events and manages the servers; the customer is billed for the execution time actually used rather than for running servers.
entries.source: General reference: widely documented cloud computing fundamentals

entries.title: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption
entries.text: Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key to encrypt and decrypt. Asymmetric encryption uses a key pair: data encrypted with the public key can be decrypted only with the matching private key.
entries.source: OWASP Top Ten and OWASP Cheat Sheet Series

entries.title: Hashing and password storage
entries.text: A cryptographic hash function is one-way: the input cannot be recovered from the hash. Passwords should be stored as salted hashes produced by a slow algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2, never in plain text.
entries.source: OWASP Top Ten and OWASP Cheat Sheet Series

entries.title: SQL injection
entries.text: SQL injection occurs when user input is concatenated into a SQL statement, letting an attacker change the query. SQL injection is prevented by using parameterised queries (prepared statements) rather than building queries from strings.
entries.source: OWASP Top Ten and OWASP Cheat Sheet Series

entries.title: Cross-site scripting
entries.text: Cross-site scripting (XSS) occurs when an application includes untrusted input in a page without escaping it, so an attacker's script runs in another user's browser. Cross-site scripting is prevented by escaping output and validating input.
entries.source: OWASP Top Ten and OWASP Cheat Sheet Series

entries.title: Authentication and authorisation
entries.text: Authentication verifies who a user is. Authorisation determines what an authenticated user is allowed to do. Multi-factor authentication requires two or more independent kinds of evidence.
entries.source: OWASP Top Ten and OWASP Cheat Sheet Series

entries.title: REST
entries.text: A REST API exposes resources at URLs and manipulates them with HTTP methods. A REST API is stateless: each request carries all the information needed to process it.
entries.source: Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures

entries.title: Caching
entries.text: A cache stores the results of expensive operations so that later requests can be served faster. Cached data can become stale, so it needs an invalidation or expiry policy.
entries.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications

entries.title: The CAP theorem
entries.text: The CAP theorem states that when a network partition occurs a distributed data store must choose between consistency and availability; it cannot guarantee both.
entries.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications

entries.title: Replication and sharding
entries.text: Replication keeps copies of the same data on several machines for availability and read throughput. Sharding (partitioning) splits the data across machines so that each holds a part of it.
entries.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications

entries.title: Message queues
entries.text: A message queue lets one service send work to another asynchronously: the producer adds messages and consumers process them later, which decouples the services and absorbs bursts of load.
entries.source: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications

entries.title: Derivative of a polynomial
entries.text: The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, and a constant factor can be taken outside the derivative. Together with the power rule, the derivative of a*x^n is a*n*x^(n-1) and the derivative of a constant is 0, so the derivative of a*x^2 + b*x + c is 2*a*x + b.
entries.source: Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals

entries.title: Derivative as a rate of change
entries.text: The derivative of a function at a point is its instantaneous rate of change there, and equals the slope of the tangent line. The derivative of position with respect to time is velocity.
entries.source: Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals

entries.title: Integral of a power
entries.text: The integral of x^n is x^(n+1)/(n+1) plus a constant of integration, for n not equal to -1. Integration is the reverse of differentiation.
entries.source: Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals

entries.title: Solving a quadratic by factoring
entries.text: A quadratic equation x^2 + b*x + c = 0 can be solved by factoring it as (x - p)(x - q) = 0, where p + q = -b and p*q = c; its solutions are x = p and x = q. A quadratic equation has at most two real solutions.
entries.source: Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals

entries.title: Prime numbers
entries.text: A prime number is an integer greater than 1 that has no positive divisors other than 1 and itself. An integer greater than 1 that is not prime is called composite.
entries.source: Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications

entries.title: Factorial definition
entries.text: For a non-negative integer n, n factorial is the product of the integers from 1 to n, and 0 factorial equals 1.
entries.source: Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications

entries.title: Logarithms
entries.text: The logarithm of x to base b is the power to which b must be raised to give x. The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms.
entries.source: Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications
